projects.title: Ransomware Dashboard
projects.oneLiner: Security teams were losing hours to fragmented alert data spread across five disconnected tools.
projects.overview: An enterprise security platform needed a single pane of glass for ransomware detection and response. I led UX for a dashboard that consolidated alert triage, asset risk, and incident timelines — cutting the time from alert to action. Details are limited under NDA, but the process and outcomes are shared below.
projects.problem: Analysts were context-switching between five tools to answer one question: "Are we under attack, and where?" Critical alerts were buried in noise, asset risk had no shared visual language, and handoffs between shifts lost context. Every minute of triage delay widened the blast radius of an active incident.
projects.myRole: I owned end-to-end UX: stakeholder discovery, analyst shadowing sessions, information architecture, the alert-triage interaction model, and the final UI system in Figma. I worked alongside a PM, two security SMEs, and four engineers.

process.body: Shadowed [Y] security analysts through live triage shifts and mapped every tool touch, question, and dead end. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Interviewed SOC leads to understand escalation paths and what "confidence" looks like during an incident.
Synthesized research into a triage journey map and three analyst archetypes. Defined the core design principle for the product: surface severity and blast radius first, raw data second.
Explored layouts for a severity-first alert queue, an asset-graph view, and an incident timeline. Pressure-tested wireframes with SMEs against real historical incidents.

Built a clickable prototype in Figma and ran moderated usability tests with [Y] analysts. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Iterated on alert grouping and the triage drill-down based on task completion friction.
Delivered a dark-mode dashboard system with a severity-ranked queue, one-click incident context, and a component library engineers could build from without guesswork.

projects.outcome: Triage time from alert to first action dropped by [X]% in pilot testing. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Analysts described the new queue as "the first screen I trust during an incident." The design system shipped with the platform's [QUARTER/YEAR] release.

projects.title: Metra Chicago
projects.oneLiner: Chicago commuters couldn't trust the app to answer one question fast: when is my train, really?
projects.overview: A self-initiated redesign of the Metra commuter rail app. Riders were abandoning the official app for screenshots of paper schedules. I redesigned the core trip flow around real-time trust — live status first, schedules second — and validated it with actual commuters on actual platforms.
projects.problem: The existing app buried real-time train status three taps deep behind a static schedule lookup. During delays — exactly when riders need the app most — it offered no proactive communication. Riders compensated with Twitter searches, platform announcements, and guesswork.
projects.myRole: Solo project: research plan, rider interviews, competitive analysis of transit apps, IA restructure, wireframes through high-fidelity UI, and usability testing.

process.body: Interviewed [Y] daily commuters and intercepted riders at Union Station during a delay event. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Audited the existing app's task flows and benchmarked against Transit, Citymapper, and Caltrain's app.

Mapped the commuter journey and found the emotional low point: standing on a platform with no signal about whether to wait or reroute. Reframed the product goal from "look up schedules" to "decide with confidence."
Sketched a home screen built around the rider's saved line: live status, next three departures, and delay context in plain language — before any menu or map.
Ran task-based usability tests with [Y] riders on a Figma prototype. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] The "should I wait or reroute" scenario drove two major iterations of the delay-state design.
Delivered a high-fidelity redesign: a status-first home, a one-tap trip board for saved routes, and a delay state that tells riders what happened and what to do next.

projects.outcome: Task completion time for "find my next train's real status" fell from [X] taps to one. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Test participants rated trust in delay information [X]/5, up from [X]/5 with the current app.

projects.title: Bond Beyond
projects.oneLiner: Long-distance families wanted to feel close, but every app reduced connection to a notification badge.
projects.overview: Bond Beyond is a mobile app concept for families separated by distance and time zones. I designed an experience built on shared rituals — not feeds — so a grandmother in Mysore and a grandkid in Chicago can feel present in each other's day without scheduling a call.
projects.problem: Existing tools force families into either high-effort video calls or low-meaning likes. Time zones make synchronous connection rare, and generic social feeds bury family moments under everything else. The result: people who love each other most interact the least.
projects.myRole: I owned the product concept, user research, journey mapping, interaction design, and the full UI system — from first interviews to a tested high-fidelity prototype.

process.body: Interviewed [Y] people in long-distance family relationships across three time zones. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Mapped when, where, and why connection attempts fail — most died in the scheduling step.

Synthesized findings into a core insight: families don't need more communication channels, they need asynchronous rituals. Defined three ritual archetypes — shared meals, daily questions, and passed-along photos.
Wireframed a ritual-first home screen and a "family table" metaphor for shared async moments. Deliberately removed follower counts, feeds, and read receipts.

Tested the prototype with [Y] family pairs over a simulated week. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Iterated on the daily-ritual flow after observing that prompts needed to feel like invitations, not chores.
Delivered a warm, low-pressure UI: a shared family space, time-zone-aware nudges, and rituals that survive a missed day without guilt mechanics.

projects.outcome: In week-long testing, [X]% of family pairs completed a ritual on at least [X] days. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Participants described the app as "a kitchen table, not a feed" — the exact feeling the design set out to create.

projects.title: The Seasoned Women
projects.oneLiner: A growing food community had loyal readers but a website that hid its best recipes behind cluttered navigation.
projects.overview: The Seasoned Women is a culinary content platform celebrating home cooking by women across generations. I redesigned the web experience end-to-end — restructuring navigation around how people actually search for recipes and giving the brand an editorial visual identity worthy of its content.
projects.problem: Readers arrived from social media for one recipe and left immediately: navigation was organized by internal categories, not cooking intent. Recipe pages buried ingredients under long preambles, and the visual design undersold the warmth of the brand. Bounce rate was high and repeat visits low.
projects.myRole: I led UX and UI: content audit, card sorting with readers, IA redesign, responsive layouts, the recipe-page template, and a lightweight design system handed off to the development team.

process.body: Ran a content audit of [Y] recipes and analyzed traffic patterns. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Conducted card-sorting sessions with [Y] readers to learn how home cooks actually categorize food: by meal, mood, and time available — not cuisine taxonomy.
Defined two primary journeys: "I have 30 minutes and these ingredients" and "I'm browsing for the weekend." Every IA and layout decision was tested against those two intents.
Wireframed an intent-based navigation, a jump-to-recipe pattern that respects the writer's story without hostage-taking the reader, and editorial landing pages for seasonal collections.

Usability-tested the responsive prototype with [Y] readers across mobile and desktop. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] Refined the recipe template after watching cooks use phones with flour-covered hands — bigger taps, sticky ingredients.
Delivered a warm editorial design system — serif display type, generous photography, intent-first navigation — plus a recipe template optimized for the kitchen counter.

projects.outcome: Post-launch, pages per session rose [X]% and recipe-page bounce rate dropped [X]%. [REPLACE WITH REAL METRIC] The team now publishes directly into the new template system without designer involvement.
